content: Healthcare providers must adhere to universal precautions and implement proper waste disposal procedures to ensure safety and hygiene. Additionally, it is imperative that providers prioritize the protection of clients' confidentiality and privacy at all times. To achieve this, all staff members should receive comprehensive training in biological and chemical safety measures. At each testing site, one designated staff member should serve as the safety focal point. This individual will be responsible for developing a biosafety manual that outlines safety protocols, including post-exposure procedures, and ensuring that all staff are familiar with its contents. Quality assurance in HIV testing is not a one-time activity but a continuous process. Providers and program managers must regularly monitor and evaluate their services to identify areas for improvement. Maintaining an effective Quality Management System (QMS) requires the involvement of all stakeholders at national, subnational, facility, and community levels. This collaborative approach ensures that the QMS addresses the specific concerns and needs of each level. Over the past two decades, middleand low-income countries have implemented various quality improvement (QI) methods in healthcare. The choice of QI method for HIV testing services (HTS) should be informed by the country’s specific context, the commitment of policymakers and program managers, and the complexity of the challenges being addressed. Case studies of quality management in HIV services in lowand middle-income countries are documented in the WHO technical brief titled Maintaining and Improving Quality of Care within HIV Clinical Services. These examples provide valuable insights into effective strategies for enhancing service quality. The WHO has also published numerous resources to support quality assurance and improvement in HIV testing services. These include guidelines for the procurement of in vitro diagnostics, handbooks for improving HIV testing and counseling services, and tools for laboratory quality management and stepwise implementation. These resources emphasize the importance of ensuring the reliability and accuracy of test results, as well as the need for robust post-market surveillance of diagnostic devices. In addition, the WHO has developed frameworks and strategic documents to guide the implementation of HIV self-testing, caregiver-assisted testing, and other innovative approaches. These resources highlight the importance of tailoring testing strategies to the needs and preferences of specific populations, including children, key populations, and individuals accessing pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP). The WHO’s consolidated guidelines on HIV testing services provide a comprehensive overview of best practices and recommendations for improving the quality and accessibility of testing services. These guidelines are supported by systematic reviews, modeling studies, and case examples that demonstrate the impact of quality assurance measures on HIV outcomes. Overall, the continuous improvement of HIV testing services requires a commitment to evidence-based practices, stakeholder collaboration, and the integration of innovative approaches to meet the evolving needs of diverse populations.
